script_data.title: The Turn That Unlocked Armageddon
script_data.description: One wrong turn. One waiting assassin. One spark that ignited the deadliest war in human history.
script_data.script:
The morning of June 28, 1914, in Sarajevo, began with regal pomp and a brush with death. Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his beloved wife Sophie, were making an official visit. As their motorcade advanced, a bomb, thrown by an assassin named Nedeljko Čabrinović, exploded behind their car, injuring several members of their entourage and onlookers. Shaken but remarkably composed, Ferdinand insisted on continuing to the planned reception at the Town Hall.

After the tense reception, Ferdinand, displaying both stubbornness and concern, made a critical decision: he would visit the wounded officers in the hospital. This selfless detour, however, necessitated an immediate change to the planned route. The new instruction, intended to bypass the city center's narrow, bustling streets, was to follow the wide Appel Quay directly to the hospital. Yet, this crucial update wasn't clearly or quickly communicated to all the drivers.

As the Archduke's lead driver, Leopold Lojka, guided the open-top Gräf & Stift automobile through the teeming streets, he reached the Latin Bridge. Instead of continuing straight along the Quay as per the *revised* plan, he instinctively took a right turn onto Franz Josef Street—the original, pre-bombing route that would have taken them through the denser heart of the city. It was a simple, understandable error born from incomplete information and the day's earlier chaos.

Mere moments later, Lojka's superior, riding in the car, shouted, "Stop! You’ve gone the wrong way!" Lojka slammed on the brakes, attempting to reverse the large vehicle. In that precise instant, the car stalled. And there, frozen in an impossible alignment, it sat. Directly in front of Moritz Schiller’s deli, nursing his dejection after the earlier failed plot, stood a young Bosnian Serb nationalist: Gavrilo Princip. He had given up hope, convinced the day was a failure, but fate, in the form of a wrong turn, had placed his target literally meters away.

Princip couldn't believe his luck. Reaching for his Browning pistol, he stepped forward, fired two shots. One struck Sophie, killing her instantly. The second hit Ferdinand, severing his jugular vein. Within minutes, the Archduke, too, lay dead. 

This single, seemingly minor navigational error wasn't just a misdirection on a street; it was the precise, improbable pivot point in history. Had Lojka gone straight, Princip would never have had his chance. The assassination would likely have failed. But because of one wrong turn, the spark that ignited World War I was struck. Within weeks, diplomatic crises escalated into open conflict, plunging Europe into a brutal war that claimed millions of lives, toppled ancient empires, redrew maps, and laid the groundwork for revolutions, fascism, and the very shape of the 20th century. A wrong turn, an impossible coincidence, and the world was irrevocably changed forever.
